Vincent van Gogh. The Dutch Post-Impressionist painter whose tormented psychology and radical use of color transformed painting into a vehicle for subjective emotional expression.

Van Gogh was born in Groot-Zundert in 1853 and worked multiple jobs—as a missionary, laborer, and clerk—before becoming an artist in his late twenties. He burned with intensity and a desperate desire for meaningful work. When he finally turned to painting, he worked for only about a decade, but that decade changed everything.

His first masterwork was The Potato Eaters in 1885, a dark, empathetic painting of peasant laborers. He rendered them with unflinching realism but gave them powerful psychological presence, establishing his commitment to expressing inner life through paint. By 1886, he moved to Paris, where he encountered Impressionism and Post-Impressionist colleagues, particularly Paul Gauguin. Gauguin's symbolic use of color and form profoundly influenced van Gogh's developing style, and together they became central figures in the Post-Impressionist movement that he would come to epitomize.

Van Gogh developed a personal color theory in which hues express emotion directly. Yellows conveyed warmth and spiritual truth, blues expressed sorrow, and reds and greens embodied passionate conflict. Color became language, not optical accuracy. His brushwork became increasingly urgent and visible, with agitated, directional strokes that seemed to convey psychological turbulence. Paint itself became an expressive medium, not merely a vehicle for representation. This urgency of gesture essentially invented the twentieth-century Expressionist movement, a movement entirely prefigured by his own radical innovations.

During his Arles period from 1888 to 1889, van Gogh painted obsessively—sunflowers, irises, starry nights, self-portraits—producing some of Western art's most iconic works in a state of feverish inspiration and psychological crisis. His mutilation of his own ear in 1888 and subsequent psychiatric hospitalization became inseparable from his legend, but they reveal only part of his story. Over eight hundred letters, primarily to his brother Theo, reveal his intellectual sophistication and conscious artistic philosophy. He was not a naive genius but a thinking artist who understood exactly what he was doing.

Van Gogh died in apparent suicide at age thirty-seven, leaving behind nearly two thousand works that were completely unknown to the public. His influence on twentieth-century art—on Expressionism, Fauvism, and modern psychology—became immeasurable posthumously. His legacy demonstrates a profound truth: art need not transcribe optical reality to communicate profound emotional truth. It can distort, intensify, and express the interior life of the maker. Artistic genius need not produce technically polished or naturalistic images. Authenticity of feeling and radical formal innovation matter more than academic skill or social success.
